subproblem.title: Derivative of the radial cutoff mass t -> integral phi(|x - y|/t) dmu (Simon Ch. 4, 4.3)
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (y : Amb n ℓ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), 0 < T → μ (closedBall y S) < ⊤ → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → (∀ u : ℝ, T ≤ u → φ u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → Integrable (fun x => φ (‖x - y‖ / t)) μ ∧ Integrable (fun x => ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t)) μ ∧ HasDerivAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) ∂μ) (-(∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) ∂μ) / t) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1, 2 and 3 of the parent proof (Simon, Ch. 4, 4.3: differentiation of the cutoff mass I(t) = integral phi(r/t) dmu), stated for one radius t. Notation: r(x) := |x - y|, phi' := deriv phi, B_S(y) the closed ball, nu := mu restricted to B_S(y).

1. Properties of phi.
 (a) phi is C^1, so phi and phi' are continuous (ContDiff.continuous_deriv). phi is differentiable with derivative phi'(u) at every u (ContDiff.differentiable).
 (b) phi'(u) = 0 for u > T. The open set (T, infinity) is a neighbourhood of u on which phi = 0, so phi coincides near u with the zero function and phi'(u) = 0 (Filter.EventuallyEq.deriv_eq).
 (c) Bounds. The continuous functions phi and u -> u phi'(u) are bounded on the compact interval [0, T] (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn): |phi(u)| <= K and |u phi'(u)| <= C for u in [0, T]. Taking u = 0 gives K >= 0 and C >= 0. For u > T, phi(u) = 0 by hypothesis and u phi'(u) = 0 by (b). Hence |phi(u)| <= K and |u phi'(u)| <= C for every u >= 0.

2. Vanishing off the ball. Let s > 0 with T s < S, and let x be outside B_S(y). Then r(x) > S > T s, so r(x)/s > T. Hence phi(r(x)/s) = 0 by hypothesis and phi'(r(x)/s) = 0 by 1(b).

3. Integrability, (a) and (b). The maps f(x) := phi(r(x)/t) and g(x) := (r(x)/t) phi'(r(x)/t) are continuous on E (compositions and products of continuous maps), hence a.e. strongly measurable for every measure. Since r(x)/t >= 0, step 1(c) gives |f| <= K and |g| <= C everywhere. As mu(B_S(y)) < infinity, f and g are integrable on B_S(y) (IntegrableOn.of_bound). By step 2 with s = t (note T t < S), f and g vanish outside B_S(y). So they are mu-integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero). This proves (a) and (b).

4. Pointwise derivative. Fix x, write r := r(x), and let s > 0. The map u -> r/u has derivative (0 * s - r * 1)/s^2 = -r/s^2 at s (quotient rule). By the chain rule and 1(a), u -> phi(r/u) has derivative phi'(r/s)(-r/s^2) = -((r/s) phi'(r/s))/s at s.

5. Differentiation under the integral sign for nu. nu is a finite measure, because nu(E) = mu(B_S(y)) < infinity (isFiniteMeasure_restrict). Put F(s, x) := phi(r(x)/s) and F'(s, x) := -((r(x)/s) phi'(r(x)/s))/s, and let N := (t/2, infinity), a neighbourhood of t. We check the hypotheses of hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le for nu at t, with the set N and the constant bound 2C/t:
 - for every s, x -> F(s, x) is continuous, hence nu-a.e. strongly measurable;
 - F(t, .) = f is nu-integrable, since it is mu-integrable (step 3);
 - F'(t, .) = -g/t is continuous, hence nu-a.e. strongly measurable;
 - for every x and every s in N we have s > t/2 > 0, so |F'(s, x)| = |(r/s) phi'(r/s)|/s <= C/s <= 2C/t, by 1(c) (r/s >= 0) and C >= 0;
 - the constant 2C/t is nu-integrable because nu is finite;
 - for every x and every s in N, s > 0, so u -> F(u, x) has derivative F'(s, x) at s by step 4.
 Hence s -> integral F(s, x) dnu(x) has derivative integral F'(t, x) dnu(x) at t.

6. Back to mu. Since T > 0, the condition T s < S is equivalent to s < S/T, so (0, S/T) is an open neighbourhood of t. For s in (0, S/T), step 2 shows that F(s, .) vanishes off B_S(y). Hence integral F(s, x) dmu = integral over B_S(y) of F(s, x) dmu = integral F(s, x) dnu (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero). So s -> integral F(s, x) dmu agrees with s -> integral F(s, x) dnu on a neighbourhood of t, and has the same derivative at t (HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq). By linearity (integral of a negative, division by the constant t), integral F'(t, x) dnu = -(integral g dnu)/t. Also integral g dnu = integral g dmu, because g vanishes off B_S(y) (step 2 with s = t). Therefore s -> integral phi(r(x)/s) dmu(x) has derivative -(integral (r/t) phi'(r/t) dmu)/t at t, which is (c).
proof_key_steps: phi and phi' are continuous, phi' = 0 on (T, infinity), and |phi(u)| <= K, |u phi'(u)| <= C for all u >= 0 (compactness of [0, T]).
For s > 0 with T s < S, phi(r/s) and phi'(r/s) vanish outside B_S(y).
x -> phi(r/t) and x -> (r/t) phi'(r/t) are continuous, bounded on B_S(y) (finite measure) and zero outside, hence mu-integrable.
d/ds phi(r/s) = -((r/s) phi'(r/s))/s, bounded by 2C/t for s > t/2.
Differentiation under the integral sign for the finite measure nu = mu restricted to B_S(y) (hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le).
On the neighbourhood (0, S/T) of t the mu- and nu-integrals agree; transfer the derivative (HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq) and rewrite its value as -(int (r/t) phi'(r/t) dmu)/t.

subproblem.title: Continuity of the radial cutoff pairing s -> integral phi(|x - y|/s)(x - y).H dmu (Simon Ch. 4, 4.3-4.4)
subproblem.statement: Let n, l be natural numbers, E := R^{n+l} (Euclidean space), mu a measure on E, H : E -> E, y in E, phi : R -> R and S, T, t real numbers. Write r(x) := |x - y| and B_S(y) for the closed ball of radius S about y. Assume: T > 0; H is mu-integrable on B_S(y); phi is continuous; phi(u) = 0 for every u >= T; t > 0; and T t < S. Then the function L(s) := integral_E phi(r(x)/s) ((x - y).H(x)) dmu(x) is continuous at s = t. Here L is a Bochner integral with the real inner product, and division follows Lean's convention x/0 = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (H : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (S T t : ℝ), 0 < T → IntegrableOn H (closedBall y S) μ → Continuous φ → (∀ u : ℝ, T ≤ u → φ u = 0) → 0 < t → T * t < S → ContinuousAt (fun s => ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / s) * inner ℝ (x - y) (H x) ∂μ) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof (continuity of L), with the localisation of step 2 (Simon, Ch. 4, 4.3-4.4). Notation: r(x) := |x - y|, B_S(y) the closed ball, nu := mu restricted to B_S(y), and h(x) := (x - y).H(x).

1. Bound on phi. phi is continuous on the compact interval [0, T], so there is K with |phi(u)| <= K for u in [0, T] (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn). Taking u = 0 gives K >= 0. For u > T, phi(u) = 0. Hence |phi(u)| <= K for all u >= 0.

2. Localisation. Since T > 0, T s < S iff s < S/T. So (0, S/T) is an open neighbourhood of t; it contains t because T t < S. Let s be in (0, S/T) and x outside B_S(y). Then r(x) > S > T s, so r(x)/s > T and phi(r(x)/s) = 0. Hence the integrand phi(r(x)/s) h(x) vanishes off B_S(y), and
 L(s) = integral over B_S(y) of phi(r(x)/s) h(x) dmu = integral phi(r(x)/s) h(x) dnu(x) =: L_nu(s)
 (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero). So L = L_nu on a neighbourhood of t, and it suffices to show that L_nu is continuous at t (ContinuousAt.congr).

3. Dominated continuity. Apply continuousAt_of_dominated to F(s, x) := phi(r(x)/s) h(x), with respect to nu at t and with the bound G(x) := K S |H(x)|.
 - Measurability. H is nu-integrable (this is the hypothesis that H is mu-integrable on B_S(y)), hence nu-a.e. strongly measurable. So x -> (x - y, H(x)) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable into E x E. The inner product is continuous on E x E, so h is nu-a.e. strongly measurable (Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable with continuous_inner). For every s, x -> phi(r(x)/s) is continuous. Hence each F(s, .) is nu-a.e. strongly measurable.
 - Domination. Take s in the neighbourhood (0, infinity) of t and x in B_S(y), which covers nu-a.e. x (ae_restrict_mem). Then r(x)/s >= 0, so |phi(r(x)/s)| <= K by step 1. Also |h(x)| <= |x - y| |H(x)| <= S |H(x)|, by Cauchy-Schwarz (norm_inner_le_norm) and |x - y| <= S. Hence |F(s, x)| <= K S |H(x)| = G(x).
 - Integrability of the bound. |H| is nu-integrable, hence so is G = K S |H|.
 - Pointwise continuity. For every x, s -> phi(r(x)/s) h(x) is continuous at t: since t != 0, s -> r(x)/s is continuous at t, phi is continuous, and h(x) is a constant.
 Therefore L_nu is continuous at t.

4. By step 2, L agrees with L_nu on a neighbourhood of t, so L is continuous at t.

On the neighbourhood (0, S/T) of t the integrand vanishes off B_S(y), so L equals its integral against nu = mu restricted to B_S(y).

ContinuousAt.congr transfers continuity from the nu-integral to L.
